account: In a series published online on 4 July 2025, Rudy and colleagues describe 17 cases involving 19 patients from seven institutions in which Face2Gene changed clinicians’ testing decisions. The full article reports that clinicians used DeepGestalt, sometimes with Feature Matcher, to analyze photographs and phenotype terms. Cases 1–3 prompted additional testing, and Cases 4–17 narrowed the testing approach. In Case 3, a strong KBG match prompted a different ANKRD11 assay after an inconclusive exome, which revealed an intragenic deletion. In Case 10, a Cornelia de Lange suggestion led to a panel that included NIPBL, which the originally considered panel omitted. Cases 5–7 illustrate targeted testing after insurance barriers to broader sequencing. The authors selected cases retrospectively from clinicians’ recollections of changed decisions, so the series does not estimate success rates across all consultations. One author was affiliated with FDNA. Independent work places the series in context. Shortly before the series appeared, Wenderott and colleagues at Bonn reported on 23 May 2025 that ten of 15 German geneticists whom they interviewed used Face2Gene in routine care, and that nine used it before molecular testing. Bruwer and colleagues reported on 27 August 2026 that DeepGestalt named the confirmed diagnosis first for only 19% of 36 South African children with a molecular diagnosis.

ai_role.statement: DeepGestalt supplied ranked facial matches, sometimes combined with phenotype terms through Feature Matcher. Clinicians used those suggestions to add or narrow molecular tests and interpreted the results. The original full-text series documents successful changes in selected cases, including alternative testing after a negative exome, but its retrospective selection does not establish general diagnostic accuracy.

fields.account: In a series published online on 4 July 2025, Rudy and colleagues describe 17 cases involving 19 patients from seven institutions in which Face2Gene changed clinicians’ testing decisions. The full article reports that clinicians used DeepGestalt, sometimes with Feature Matcher, to analyze photographs and phenotype terms. Cases 1–3 prompted additional testing, and Cases 4–17 narrowed the testing approach. In Case 3, a strong KBG match prompted a different ANKRD11 assay after an inconclusive exome, which revealed an intragenic deletion. In Case 10, a Cornelia de Lange suggestion led to a panel that included NIPBL, which the originally considered panel omitted. Cases 5–7 illustrate targeted testing after insurance barriers to broader sequencing. The authors selected cases retrospectively from clinicians’ recollections of changed decisions, so the series does not estimate success rates across all consultations. One author was affiliated with FDNA. Independent work places the series in context. Shortly before the series appeared, Wenderott and colleagues at Bonn reported on 23 May 2025 that ten of 15 German geneticists whom they interviewed used Face2Gene in routine care, and that nine used it before molecular testing. Bruwer and colleagues reported on 27 August 2026 that DeepGestalt named the confirmed diagnosis first for only 19% of 36 South African children with a molecular diagnosis.
fields.summary: Face2Gene's DeepGestalt facial analysis changed geneticists' testing decisions in 17 retrospectively selected cases involving 19 patients, leading to confirmed diagnoses.

purpose: Face2Gene is built to suggest candidate syndromes from facial photographs and clinical features so that geneticists can direct testing. Changed testing decisions were that purpose.

ratings.reason: DeepGestalt changed medical geneticists' testing decisions in 17 cases involving 19 patients. The full article reports confirmed diagnoses in selected cases, such as an intragenic ANKRD11 deletion found after an inconclusive exome.
The authors claim “a more efficient test strategy”, and Cases 5–7 illustrate targeted testing after insurance barriers to broader sequencing. No source counts tests avoided or time saved.
